Circle defends USDC economics as stablecoin rivals court its partners with bigger cut. Circle defends USDC economics as stablecoin rivals court its partners with bigger cut
Coinbase, Circle’s largest USDC partner, also backs Open USD, a rival network that passes reserve income to partners after a management fee.
- Circle said it kept about 7 cents of profit per revenue dollar in the first half of 2026, after $819 million of $1.4 billion went to distribution and transaction costs.
- Coinbase, Circle’s largest USDC partner, also backs Open USD, a rival network that passes reserve income to partners after a management fee.
- Circle argued reserve income must also fund redemption, compliance and liquidity, and says standard USDC redemptions remain free.
Stablecoin issuer Circle 
In a blog post on Friday, Chief Commercial Officer Kash Razzaghi wrote that Circle kept about 7 cents in net profit for each dollar in revenue made during the first half of 2026. The firm brought in about $1.4 billion, while distribution and transaction costs totaled $819 million.
The post puts the figures at the center of a dispute over who gets the interest earned on assets backing stablecoins.
Circle said the remaining $473 million covered compliance, liquidity and product development. That figure also included about $214 million in stock-based compensation and related costs.
Coinbase is Circle’s largest USDC partner, but is also a backer of Open USD, along with Stripe and BlackRock. Open USD, unveiled in June, aims to let businesses mint and redeem stablecoins without fees, while passing off reserve income minus a management fee to participants.
Circle's post did not name Open USD, whose OUSD token is now live, directly, and there are other competitors like the Paxos-led Global Dollar Network (USDG) that also share reserve income with participants.
"The costs of redemption, compliance, and resilience don't disappear just because the issuer declined to pay them," Razzaghi wrote.
Circle has also been working to secure additional distribution partners. In September, Binance bought a $100 million stake in the firm under a five-year deal that includes a fee tied to USDC held through Circle's wallet service.
Circle said standard USDC redemptions remain free and "typically settle in up to two business days." Qualifying platform customers and payment flows through Circle Payments Network can now access near-real-time redemptions at no cost, it said.

Citrini sees a tokenization boom. The harder question is who profits. Citrini sees a tokenization boom. The harder question is who profits
The influential research firm says real-world assets could finally give blockchains a clear role in finance. For investors, the next challenge is figuring out which companies, networks and protocols capture the revenue.
This is an excerpt from CoinDesk's new ‘Tokenization Weekly’ newsletter that will be launching soon. Sign-up details will be here when it goes live.
Crypto enthusiasts have spent years telling that finance – stocks, bonds and other financial assets – would eventually move onto blockchains.
Now, an influential research firm that Wall Street investors pay attention to has made the case for them.
Citrini Research, better known for its work on broader technology, AI and market trends than for cheerleading crypto, turned its attention last week to tokenization in a 79-page report titled Breaking the Wall.
The report itself isn't news anymore, but the argument behind it is worth sitting with because it marks how far the conversation has moved.
For years, crypto built increasingly sophisticated infrastructure for trading, lending and moving money, while most of the assets investors actually wanted to own — stocks, bonds, credit and commodities — stayed inside the traditional financial system. Now those assets are beginning to migrate onto the rails crypto spent more than a decade building.
Citrini summed it up in one line:
“Blockchains have finally found their raison d’être.”
Why it matters
For better or worse, one of the oldest knocks on crypto and blockchains was that it looked like a solution in search of a problem.
There were decentralized exchanges, automated lending protocols, crypto wallets and increasingly elaborate financial plumbing, but if all of it was mainly being used to trade one cryptocurrency against other cryptocurrency, the obvious question remained: what was the infrastructure actually built for?
Tokenization may finally provide a convincing answer.
U.S. Treasuries, credit, stocks, funds and other assets are increasingly moving onchain, and once they are there, the point isn't simply that an investor can trade Nvidia at 2 a.m on a Sunday.
The more interesting argument Citrini made is that tokenization can make financial assets behave more like software: moving between applications, serving as collateral, being borrowed against or plugged into other financial products without each platform rebuilding custody and settlement from scratch.
Those pieces are also starting to come together. Stablecoins put cash onchain. Wallets, exchanges and DeFi protocols have matured. Retail-facing trading platforms like Robinhood (HOOD), Coinbase (COIN) and others bring distribution. And regulators – in the U.S. and around the globe – are beginning to give tokenized securities a clearer path into markets.
Why this is a big deal
Citrini isn't discovering tokenization. Crypto-native investors have talked about real-world assets (RWA) for years.
What's different is seeing a widely followed research shop outside the crypto bubble translate the thesis into the language that large investors care about most: where do you actually make money?
That isn't as obvious as it sounds.
Citrini argued that tokenization could lift the broader crypto ecosystem, but more assets moving onchain doesn't automatically make bitcoin 
Arthur Hayes, BitMEX's co-founder and the chief investment officer of Maelstrom, framed that problem more bluntly.
RWA tokenization has been talked about for a decade, he said in a recent interview with The Rollup, and simply taking a security that already sits in a digital database and recording it somewhere else doesn't necessarily create much value.
“Okay, doing better bookkeeping. Thank you,” Hayes said. “Where are you actually going to make money in tokenization?”
There are several possible answers.
Tokenized stocks can generate issuance fees, trading revenue, stablecoin demand, lending activity and collateral usage, but those economics can land in very different places.
Christian Magoon, CEO of Amplify ETFs, which runs the tokenization-focused TKNQ fund, thinks infrastructure providers could become “toll booths on the blockchain toll roads,” while distribution may be just as valuable: Coinbase, Robinhood, banks and wealth platforms who already have the customer relationships.
Jeff Dorman, CIO of investment firm Arca, told CoinDesk he expects the actual tokenization process to become increasingly commoditized as competition grows.
The stickier economics, he said, emerge after an asset is onchain: when it starts trading, being lent out or serving as collateral to borrow. That's why he sees potential beneficiaries ranging from Securitize (SECZ) to crypto protocols such as blockchain-based trading venue Hyperliquid, decentralized lender Aave 
Zach Pandl, head of digital asset research at Grayscale, told CoinDesk the simpler bet may be the networks underneath all of it.
"The most direct way to position a portfolio for the tokenization megatrend is to own the networks that host RWAs and process transactions," he said. "The industry leaders today are Ethereum 
Other networks could carve out different roles. Avalanche (AVAX) and Canton 
And that's where Hayes sees an even bigger story that could make tokenization much more than better bookkeeping: AI agents running financial services.
“I think the best story I want to tell is that AI agents will run all of your financial services,” Hayes said.
Think of software continuously rebalancing your portfolio, moving idle cash toward higher yields, finding a cheaper loan or shifting collateral as market conditions change. Those agents would need money and investments they can access programmatically, around the clock, without a human clicking through each transaction.
That happens to look a lot like the infrastructure crypto has spent years building: programmable assets, always-on markets, smart-contract lending and near-instant settlement.
Citrini landed on a similar argument, saying tokenized assets effectively translate financial products into a machine-native format that AI agents can work with.
Still, there is plenty of room for those winners to change. Amplify’s Magoon stressed that the market remains “extremely early,” with tokenized assets still tiny compared with global financial markets.
“The long runway ahead increases the likelihood that future winners may differ from today's leaders,” he said.

‘Wow, it’s a real discovery’: Claude cracks a 25-year NSA number mystery. ‘Wow, it’s a real discovery’: Claude cracks a 25-year NSA number mystery
Numbers the spy agency handed over in the 1990s, long suspected of hiding a backdoor, turn out to have come from a basic computer program. Bitcoin was never on that list, and its quantum problem hasn’t gone anywhere.
- An Anthropic AI model took less than 30 minutes to trace five unexplained seeds for NIST elliptic curves supplied by the National Security Agency to an ordinary random-number generator using timestamps from 1997 and 1998.
- The finding makes a hidden NSA backdoor less likely and does not require users of the NIST curves to take action, though questions remain about how some elements were selected.
- Bitcoin was not affected because it uses secp256k1, a simpler curve with little room to conceal a weakness, although sufficiently powerful quantum computers could eventually pose a separate threat.
An Anthropic AI model has cracked one of cryptography’s longest-running whodunits, tracing numbers the NSA handed to the U.S. government in the late 1990s, which were long suspected of hiding a backdoor, to an ordinary random-number program fed with timestamps from 1997 and 1998.
It took the model just about half an hour to come up with a solution — one that cryptographers had been chasing to answer for 25 years.
A lock with an unexplained design
Much of the internet relies on elliptic-curve cryptography, the family of mathematics that is also used to protect bitcoin wallets. It lets someone prove they hold a secret key without revealing the details of the key itself.
Think of the curve as a lock design anyone can inspect. Each person using it has their own secret key, but everyone relies on the design being difficult to break.
But who chose the mathematics everyone would trust?
In 2000, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, adopted a set of curves supplied by the National Security Agency. The NSA provided those designs without explaining where some of the numbers used to generate them came from.
The secrecy became even harder to dismiss after the Snowden disclosures linked the NSA to efforts to weaken cryptographic standards. NIST later removed that tool, the Dual EC random-number generator, from its recommendations.
Those starting numbers, called seeds, were public. But the NSA never explained how it chose them, fueling years of suspicion that it had tested many alternatives until it found a curve with a weakness only it knew how to exploit. The tinfoil theory was that the NSA had a backdoor to every system that used it.
Cryptographers Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes examined the controversy in their 2015 paper, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma.” Menezes had helped write the original standard and recalled receiving the seeds from NSA mathematician Jerry Solinas in 1997.
Security researcher Steve Weis spent years looking for an explanation, including filing public-records requests in 2018. NIST said it had no documentation, while the NSA stopped responding. One promising lead suggested the numbers came from a humorous phrase Solinas had forgotten, sending investigators searching through possible word combinations.
In 2023, cryptography engineer Filippo Valsorda and other contributors offered a $12,288 bounty for an answer, rising to over $36,000 if the winner donated it to charity. Solinas had died earlier that year, leaving researchers to work through old recollections and the numbers themselves to no outcome.
Claude goes digging
Until Claude entered the picture. This month, an Anthropic employee asked an internal research model to investigate, without sharing the old theory that the seeds came from a forgotten phrase.
It took the model less than half an hour to trace five NIST curve seeds to lrand48, a random-number generator found in older C software libraries.
Claude reproduced the sequence behind P-256, a widely used curve, and found an exact match for its published seed at the 1,842nd candidate.
“This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery,” the model wrote in its recorded reasoning, after briefly questioning whether it was working inside a simulated test. “Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world.”
“Wow, it's a real discovery.”
Anyone can now rerun the program and get the numbers the NSA supplied. Anthropic says that makes a hidden weakness much less likely, though the team still cannot explain why the program passed over some usable candidates or how other parts of the curves were chosen.
That predictability is what let Claude rebuild the numbers, and it would be a disaster inside a wallet. A secret key generated with lrand48 could be recreated by anyone who worked out roughly when it was made, giving them everything needed to drain the funds.
The NSA’s seeds were public from day one, so there was never a secret to steal.
Where bitcoin fits in
Bitcoin was never part of this guessing game. Its wallets run on secp256k1, a curve built from a simpler equation.
Bitcoin’s version is defined by two small, fixed numbers that leave almost nothing to adjust, while P-256’s version carries a 77-digit number that came out of the NSA’s unexplained seed.
With so few dials to turn, there’s little room for anyone to have quietly built a weakness into bitcoin’s curve, and cryptographers have long pointed to that as a point in its favor.
Creator Satoshi Nakamoto never publicly explained why he picked it, and the curve was rarely used before bitcoin made it famous. Ethereum later adopted it too, and bitcoin kept it when its 2021 Taproot upgrade introduced a newer style of signature.
A powerful quantum computer would bring a different danger, as CoinDesk explored earlier this year. It could work backward from a public key visible on Bitcoin’s blockchain to the secret key behind it, regardless of how the curve was chosen.
Hardware advances keep narrowing the gap between that theory and a working attack. Google said this week its Willow chip cut errors about 40-fold in one of the costliest steps such a machine would need.
Still, nobody has yet built a quantum computer anywhere near large or reliable enough to crack a bitcoin key, and there’s no clear timeline for when one might arrive.
Meanwhile, Anthropic said in its blog that people using the NIST curves do not need to change anything. After decades of questions about where the seeds came from, anyone can now run the program and retrace its path to the published numbers.
The search had a prize, too. Its $36,864 bounty will go to the Internet Security Research Group, the nonprofit behind Let’s Encrypt, which gives websites free security certificates.

Satoshi-era bitcoin faces a bigger quantum threat after Google’s new Willow breakthrough. Satoshi-era bitcoin faces a bigger quantum threat after Google’s new Willow breakthrough
Google says its Willow chip can prepare the special quantum states needed for advanced calculations with about 40 times fewer errors, reducing one of the hardware bottlenecks behind any future attempt to crack bitcoin wallets.
- Google said its Willow quantum chip reduced errors about 40-fold when preparing “magic states,” a resource needed for quantum calculations that could eventually threaten Bitcoin wallets.
- The experiment achieved about 99.99 percent fidelity among states that passed inspection, though only about 8 percent of preparation attempts succeeded and substantial scaling challenges remain.
- The findings do not make a Bitcoin attack 40 times cheaper, but they advance an engineering method that could help future quantum computers sustain the roughly 500,000 reliable magic states per second required under one modeled attack.
Google says its Willow quantum chip has cut errors about 40-fold when preparing special states used in quantum calculations, tackling a costly step toward building machines powerful enough to crack bitcoin wallets.
The result, published in Science this week, deals with something that rarely comes up in the bitcoin quantum debate — which usually focuses on how big a machine an attacker would need while underplaying how much of that machine would be occupied getting ready to calculate.
Why the oldest coins give an attacker more time
A bitcoin wallet uses a secret key to approve payments and a matching public key that lets the network check those approvals. Spending typically reveals the public key, while some payment types expose it from the start.
Working backward from it to the secret is supposed to take an impractical amount of computing, which makes it practically impossible to reverse-engineer crypto wallets.
However, a large enough quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could, in theory, do that math. Whoever recovered the secret key could sign transactions as the owner, and the network would accept them as genuine. Mathematician Peter Shor first published the method in 1994, but nobody has yet managed to demonstrate it.
A recovery phrase locked in a physical drawer offers no protection against that, as the attacker would be working from information already sitting on the blockchain.
Some later payment formats hide the public key behind a hash, a digital fingerprint, until the owner spends. An attacker targeting a previously hidden key would have to wait for that exposure and might need to recover the secret quickly enough to interfere with the payment.
That is also why lost coins present a difficult problem. Bitcoin can introduce stronger spending protections, but someone still needs the existing keys to move old holdings into them. If those keys are lost, the owner cannot make the move. The exposed public key remains available to a future attacker.
Some of bitcoin’s oldest holdings have had their public keys exposed since they were mined.
Old coins have also been moving as the quantum debate grows louder. On Oct. 7, 100.02 BTC untouched since July 2010 moved after more than 16 years, carrying a value of about $8.5 million. In August, six wallets inactive since 2011–2014 moved another 553.59 BTC, worth roughly $40 million at the time.
Those transfers do not singularly establish that holders are responding to quantum fears, as moving coins can even mean changing wallets, reorganizing holdings or preparing to sell.
The cost of getting ready
Quantum computers store information in units called qubits, which are extremely fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals can disturb them and introduce errors, and adding more qubits also adds more opportunities for mistakes.
Engineers deal with that by organizing many physical qubits into groups that detect and correct errors. Each group behaves like a more dependable unit, known as a logical qubit.
Those units then need the digital equivalent of fuel to run certain operations, specially prepared quantum states that researchers call “magic states.” Each one is consumed when used, so the computer has to keep producing them throughout a calculation.
Read More: A simple explainer on what quantum computing actually is, and why it is terrifying for bitcoin
Think of a restaurant kitchen where every dish needs a fresh batch of a sauce that cannot be reused, where some of the staff must keep making sauce while the others cook. In a quantum computer, hardware devoted to producing magic states is hardware that cannot be assigned to other work.
Google’s method, called cultivation, starts with a rough version of the state, checks it for errors and throws out flawed attempts. The goal is to produce clean states using less hardware than older methods needed.
The firm reported about 99.99% fidelity, a measure of how closely the finished states matched what researchers were aiming for.
That number applies only to the states that passed inspection. Willow kept about 8% of its attempts after the checks during preparation and measurement. For every 100 tries, about eight made it through.
The next steps include running the process at a much larger scale and keeping those states useful as they feed into longer calculations. The researchers say more work is needed on real-time operations and moving the states into stronger error-correcting setups.
How it fits with earlier research
In March, Google estimated that a future superconducting quantum computer with fewer than 500,000 physical qubits could break the wallet cryptography used by Bitcoin and Ethereum, under a specific set of hardware assumptions.
In September, CoinDesk reported on researchers cutting the workload of a core calculation used in that attack. That work covered one component, leaving out the complete attack and the physical hardware costs of running it.
Those studies reduce the amount of math an attacker has to do. Cultivation addresses the cost of supplying the machine while it does that math.
The gains cannot simply be multiplied together. Google’s March estimate already assumed efficient magic-state production. The experiment tests part of that engineering approach, rather than providing another 40-fold reduction in the estimated cost of attacking bitcoin.
The March paper also shows how much fuel an attack would burn. For one modeled attack lasting about nine minutes after a public key becomes available, Google estimated the machine would need roughly 500,000 sufficiently reliable magic states every second.
references.title: Satoshi-era bitcoin faces a bigger quantum threat after Google’s new Willow breakthrough

Live updates: Bitcoin dips to $81,000 as stocks slide, VIX soars ahead of Black Monday anniversary. VIX soars, Nasdaq sheds 2% ahead of 39-year anniversary of 1987's Black Monday market crash
Surely just a coincidence, but this coming Monday marks the 39-year anniversary of the Black Monday, October 19, 1987, stock market crash, when the S&P 500 plunged more than 20%.
That makes today the 39-year anniversary of the Friday before the 1987 crash. While not nearly as dramatic as the S&P 500’s 5% decline 39 years ago, the Nasdaq fell 2.15% today.
Alongside, the volatility index (VIX) — often referred to as the “fear gauge” — soared 22%.
Rumors were flying of someone or some group getting blown out of their positions, but nothing’s been confirmed just yet.
Bitcoin is off of its lows, but still down 1% over the past 24 hours at $81,500.
Stocks losses quickly double, with bitcoin attempting to decouple
The Nasdaq is at session lows a bit less than 90 minutes before the close of trading for the week, down 2.3%. The S&P 500 is down 1.25%.
What was a modestly negative day appears to have turned into a rout as oil prices quickly jumped about $3 per barrel over the past couple of hours. WTI crude is now up 3.8% to $101.70.
Government bonds — which benefitted earlier this week as money flowed into fixed income alongside declining stocks — aren’t seeing a bid today. The 10-year Treasury yield is near the day’s high at 5.112%.
After initially declining alongside stocks earlier on Friday, bitcoin is attempting to stabilize as equities add to losses this afternoon. It’s currently at $81,350, down 1% over the past 24 hours.
Crypto stocks slammed as oil surges, interest rates turn higher, and stocks slide
Rising slowly at first, the price of oil is headed straight up over the past few minutes, with WTI crude now up more than 3% on the day to a one-month high of $101 per barrel.
That’s up 16% over the past 10 days.
There are reports that Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline has been targeted in an attack.
U.S. government bond yields are responding; the 10-year Treasury is now higher by 3.5 basis points to 5.125% after earlier dipping to 5.07%.
The Nasdaq is lower by 1.5% and bitcoin has pulled back to $81,300.
Down earlier in the session, front-month WTI crude oil has climbed to a one-month high of $99.40 per barrel, up 1.5% on the day, with much of the move coming in the past few minutes — though there’s no particular news that’s hit the tape.
The action may be spooking the bond market, where U.S. Treasury yields have swung from declines to gains over the past hour.
U.S. refined products (gasoline and distillates) inventories, meanwhile, continue at decade lows, according to government data.
The Nasdaq is near a session low, off 1.4% for the day.
After a volatile week of trading in stocks and bonds, Friday had gotten off to a slow start, but declines are speeding up late in the U.S. morning.
The Nasdaq is now down 1.2%, led by big drops in familiar AI-related names.
Among the Mag 7, Tesla has turned lower after opening with sizable gains following its Roadster event last night. Apple is the only gainer in the group, up 1.1%.
The selling is spreading to crypto, where bitcoin has dipped about 1% over the 30 minutes to $81,500.
Fixed income is catching a bid, with the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield now barely down for the day at 5.08% after earlier rising to 5.13%.
Bounce in neoclouds proves short-lived, with CoreWeave down 8%
After days of relentless selling, the neoclouds — former bitcoin miners turned data center providers to the fast-growing AI sector — bounced hard on Thursday, many closing the day in the green after early sharp declines.
The selling has resumed on Friday, though, with CoreWeave (CRWV) lower by 8% and extending its weekly decline to more than 20%.
Hut 8, IREN, CleanSpark, Keel Infrastructure, and Cipher Mining are all down roughly 6%.
In a note on Friday, Goldman Sachs pointed out that the widening in high-yield bond spreads is an AI story: Non-AI-related spreads were barely higher this week, while AI-related spreads widened by 25 basis points.
“We view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate,” said the bank’s Amanda Lynam.
“I write to urge Anthropic to pause its planned initial public offering until the company fully and transparently addresses the artificial intelligence safety, governance, and development pace concerns it has raised,” wrote New York City Comptroller Mark Levine to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this week.
Levine noted in the letter that as comptroller, he is an investment adviser, custodian, and trustee of NYC pension funds, with more than $325 billion in assets.
Strive raises $630 million with new preferred offering
Bitcoin treasury company Strive ASST$24.10·Sarado ang Merkado upsized the offering of its new high-yielding preferred stock, SATS, to 7 million shares (from 5 million).
The sale was priced at $90 per share, giving the company gross proceeds of $630 million.
Strategy declares conditional daily dividend for STRC to begin November 1
Led by Michael Saylor, the company announced weeks ago its plan to switch to a daily dividend (from monthly) for its high-yielding preferred stock STRC.
The change is subject to a shareholder vote, which is underway, and the results will be known on Oct. 28.
Today’s announcement is thus conditional on the vote being in favor of the move to daily payments.
While strongly rebounding from its panicky lows of early summer, STRC continues to trade just below par value (yesterday’s close was $99.53), leaving Saylor and team unable to raise bitcoin-buying capital by issuing more shares.
Warsh isn't ruling out October rate hike, but markets mostly have
“I don’t prejudge meetings,” said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking at a fireside chat overnight at an IMF event. “I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have."
“It’s a new chapter at the Fed, and we’re not in that business anymore.”
Warsh defended the September rate hike as a necessary move to cool inflation.
He said the AI boom was the most important thing happening to global economies now, and said it was likely creating price pressures. Productivity gains will come, he said, but the road will be bumpy.
Rates are modestly higher from yesterday’s close, the 10-year U.S. yield up 2.9 basis points to 5.12%.
October Fed rate hikes odds have dipped to 15% from nearly 45% in the moments after the CPI report on Wednesday.
Crypto selloff after inflation report is temporary, Binance's Catherine Chen says
The latest inflation-driven crypto selloff is a short-term reaction rather than a sign of deeper trouble, according to Catherine Chen, Binance's head of institutional.
“The CPI-driven selloff is a sentiment shock, not a structural break,” Chen said, referring to the Consumer Price Index, a measure of U.S. inflation.
Chen expects inflation to peak around October, with clearer signs of cooling potentially emerging in March 2027. Lower energy prices and easing inflation could eventually help crypto markets recover, she said.
“A difficult trading day does not determine the outlook for the next several months,” Chen added. “The window for relief may already be approaching.”
Bitcoin climbed back above $82,000 on Friday, a day after a brief drop under $80,000, as ZEC led a broad crypto bounce with an 11% jump to about $1,230 — even as investors pulled money from the token’s only U.S. ETF.
SOL and ether each gained more than 3%, to about $106 and $2,450, and DOGE and XRP added between 2% and 3%. BNB, HYPE and TRX rose about 1%, and bitcoin was up nearly 1%, according to CoinDesk data.
The bounce hasn’t reached the ETFs. The U.S. spot ZEC fund lost about $15 million on Thursday, its fifth outflow this month, according to SoSoValue data. Ether funds shed about $60 million, and SOL funds lost nearly $10 million, their ninth straight day of withdrawals. XRP funds saw a small outflow.
Bitcoin ETFs drew a net $5 million, a thin inflow after Wednesday’s $261 million exit.
A second straight day of bitcoin ETF inflows would be the first sign the bounce from $80,000 has buyers behind it.

An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own. An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own
The research model derived funded Sepolia addresses from public seed phrases, questioned whether using the money was ethical, then called the funds “effectively abandoned” and used them anyway.
- An internal OpenAI research model used a publicly available recovery phrase to access and spend from another person’s cryptocurrency wallet after it ran out of funds during a coding assignment.
- The June 26 incident occurred on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network, whose tokens have no connection to ether traded on the main network, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25.
- The model completed the assignment without disclosing the source of the funds, prompting OpenAI to add internet-access restrictions and increased monitoring.
An OpenAI research model stuck without funds on an Ethereum test network went looking for someone else’s wallet, found one through recovery phrases that were already public, and spent from it to finish a coding assignment, the company disclosed Thursday.
The incident occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25, according to its incident report.
The model needed no hacking skills to get in.
A recovery phrase, also called a seed phrase, is a list of words that generates a wallet’s secret keys; whoever has those words can recreate the accounts and spend from them without ever touching the owner’s device.
The assignment let the model deploy contracts, programs that run on a blockchain, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the fees. After its attempts to get free test tokens failed, it wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers and found one with enough money.
“But using public known key/funds ethically?” the model asked itself in its recorded reasoning, before deciding that a public phrase and test tokens made it acceptable.
The spending happened on Sepolia, a separate network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications before launching them. Its tokens only pay for testing and aren't linked to the ether traded on Ethereum’s main network.
The deployment went through, and the wallet paid the fees. When the model reported back, it said the work was done and left out where the money came from. OpenAI said it has since added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring.
Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person signing off on each step.
OpenAI’s model ran out of money mid-task, found a wallet that wasn’t its own and spent from it without asking. Had it been on Ethereum’s main network, that would have been real ether taken from someone else’s account.

Banks could slow stablecoin growth by paying savers more, BIS paper finds. Banks could slow stablecoin growth by paying savers more, BIS paper finds
A BIS working paper found a 1 basis point rise in U.S. bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth, cutting ten-week growth from 15% to 12%.
- A BIS working paper found a 1 basis point rise in U.S. bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth, cutting ten-week growth from 15% to 12%.
- The effect was stronger for Circle's USDC than Tether's USDT, which the authors linked to USDC's closer ties to U.S. users.
- The authors say banks retain some influence over stablecoin adoption through deposit pricing, though the sample covers only one high-rate period.
Banks may be able to slow the growth of stablecoins like USDT and USDC by paying savers more, according to a working paper published by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
Researchers Rashad Ahmed and Iñaki Aldasoro studied weekly data from January 2019 to June 2025, accounting for bitcoin prices, Treasury yields and broader financial conditions. They found that a one-week, one basis point rise in average bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth.
That small figure, just 0.01 percentage points, cut average ten-week growth in stablecoin market capitalization from about 15% to about 12%, the paper found.
Under the authors’ preferred estimate, which adjusts for banks raising rates in response to stablecoin growth, the effect was roughly three times larger, slowing growth to about 6%, though the authors flagged some weakness in that method. In both cases, growth slowed but did not reverse.
The relationship was stronger for Circle’s USDC than Tether’s USDT, a pattern the authors said was consistent with USDC’s closer ties to U.S. users.
The findings add evidence to a debate that has drawn warnings from bank executives. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan warned in January that as much as $6 trillion in deposits could move into stablecoins and related products offering returns, potentially reducing lending capacity and raising borrowing costs.
The effect is partly based on where issuers put their reserves. A December Federal Reserve staff analysis explained that money placed in stablecoins can return to banks as issuer deposits, changing who supplies banks’ funding even when total deposits remain unchanged.
Larger, uninsured balances could require banks to keep more liquid assets and leave less room for long-term loans that financial institutions issue.
Paying more to retain customers also raises banks’ funding costs. The Fed analysis suggested banks could target better rates at customers most likely to switch, while keeping lower rates for less mobile depositors.
The BIS paper does not establish losses of bank deposits or lending. Its sample covers one high-rate episode, and the findings may change as yield-bearing stablecoins and tokenized money market funds gain ground.
Banks “retain some influence over the pace of that adoption through deposit pricing,” the authors wrote.

A 10-minute flush hit round-the-clock chip-stock contracts while U.S. markets were shut, leaving traders with no real share price to lean on.
- Nearly $52 million in leveraged bets tied to chip stocks and semiconductor funds were liquidated in 10 minutes Saturday, even as Wall Street was closed.
- The sell-off began on Binance and spread within seconds to Hyperliquid, with traders betting on higher prices accounting for about $38 million of the liquidations.
- Because the contracts trade around the clock, weekend prices were driven by crypto traders rather than actual share prices, which will provide a benchmark when U.S. markets reopen Monday.
A sudden wave of selling wiped out nearly $52 million in crypto traders’ leveraged bets on chip stocks in 10 minutes on Saturday, while the shares themselves sat idle with Wall Street closed for the weekend.
Those bets were placed through perpetual futures, contracts that track a stock’s price and trade around the clock on crypto exchanges, so traders can buy and sell chip stocks on a Saturday night.
A trader who borrows to make a bigger bet gets closed out automatically when losses eat through their deposit, and the forced selling can push prices lower for the next trader in line.

Stablecoin supply has barely budged this year, but the digital dollars already in circulation are doing more work in payments, according to a fresh report from blockchain analytics firm Allium.
Stablecoin payments are growing at a rapid pace, reaching $482 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% from a year earlier, the report found.
That growth contrasts with the broader stablecoin market. The total value of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies tied to fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar — in circulation stood at about $305 billion at the end of September, up a meager 0.4% since the start of the year, according to the report.
The number of payments grew even more, jumping 71% to over 1 billion, the report said, suggesting that stablecoins are changing hands more often without much new supply entering the market.
Stablecoin-linked cards showed some of the fastest growth. Spending measured by Allium reached $3.9 billion through September, ten times the amount a year earlier. Small purchases — under $50 — accounted for 84% of the increase in card transactions.
Stablecoins meet traditional payment rails
Three announcements earlier this week offered a glimpse of how stablecoins are becoming increasingly part of global payments.
Mastercard (MA) introduced Thursday its Global Money Platform with BVNK, the stablecoin infrastructure firm it acquired in August. The service combines traditional currency accounts, stablecoin balances, conversions, card spending and bank payouts through one connection.
Banks and fintechs can use the platform to offer accounts that hold both fiat currencies and stablecoins, the firm said. Payments firms Nuvei and Marqeta are among the first customers integrating that service.
Stripe, meanwhile, is working with Plasma 
The companies said they plan to let customers spend from the balance that matches their purchase, cutting unnecessary currency conversions. Stripe's expanded card infrastructure covers more than 30 countries, with plans to reach over 100 by next year.

And Visa (V) said it is bringing stablecoins into the funding side of international payments.
The company said Inyo Global, a payment orchestration firm for fintech, money transmitter, banks, became the first provider to put Visa Direct's stablecoin prefunding service into commercial use. Payment firms can use Circle's (CRCL) dollar stablecoin USDC

That rapid growth of stablecoin payments comes with some caveats. Of $97.9 trillion in raw stablecoin transfers through September, Allium classified just $2.4 trillion, or 2.5%, as end-user activity after filtering out exchange, decentralized finance and automated transactions. Its $482 billion payments estimate comes from that smaller pool, the report said.

For payment companies, that leaves a large market to pursue. Nuvei CEO Phil Fayer, whose company is among the first to integrate Mastercard's new platform, said stablecoins are becoming part of how businesses move money across borders and currencies.
"The future of global commerce depends on money moving as freely as the businesses and consumers it serves, across borders, currencies and increasingly, between traditional and digital forms of money," Fayer said.

Ryan Rasmussen, head of research at Bitwise, expects bitcoin to emerge from the coming weeks’ uncertainty at a higher valuation.

He identified three longer-term drivers: institutional buying through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and corporate purchases; demand for hard assets amid inflation, rising debt and currency debasement; and clearer regulation that reduces the perceived risk of owning crypto.

Rasmussen nevertheless expects volatility around a possible late-October Federal Reserve rate increase and November’s U.S. midterm elections. A breakout would be difficult in that environment, he said, although the uncertainty could create an opportunity for investors to build positions.
Adam Morgan McCarthy, head of research at LO:TECH, a London-based crypto trading and market data firm, is more cautious. His base case is an $85,000–$95,000 trading range into year-end.
“Macro has gone against Bitcoin all year, with the Fed hiking in September and a December hike priced at roughly 75%,” McCarthy said. “This will continue to weigh on bitcoin.”

Positioning offers more encouragement. Leverage has largely been flushed out of bitcoin, with much of the speculative excess moving into altcoins, Invernizzi said.
McCarthy also sees fewer crowded bullish positions that could unravel. Funding rates, payments between perpetual futures traders, are at or below zero, while August’s rally was driven by traders closing bearish bets rather than adding new bullish positions.
That reduces the fuel for forced selling and leaves room for another squeeze higher.
“A clean break above $90K for BTC could trigger another round of short covering,” Invernizzi said.

The team behind Zakura wants every swap through NEAR Intents to get its own key, so a refund address left on NEAR’s public chain can’t expose a user’s wider payment history.
- Zakura wants to assign a separate viewing key to every ZEC swap made through NEAR Intents, limiting the payment history that a future quantum computer could uncover from a publicly posted refund address.
- The proposal would keep spending keys with users while using private information retrieval to help wallets locate refunds without revealing which addresses they are checking.
- Zakura says compatible software wallets could adopt the open-source feature within weeks, before Zcash developers’ January target for quantum-resistant payments.
The team behind Zakura, a newer version of the software that runs the Zcash network, wants to give every ZEC swap made through NEAR Intents its own private key.
The change would close a gap that a future quantum computer could use to piece together a user’s payment history, according to a new engineering post from the team.
NEAR Intents is a service that lets users swap tokens across different blockchains. When someone swaps private ZEC for USDC through it, the service posts one of their private Zcash addresses on NEAR’s public chain, so it knows where to send back any unused ZEC. That address goes up as soon as the deposit lands and stays there even if the swap goes through and no refund is ever needed.
Such addresses give away no information on today’s computers. Each Zcash address carries a public key built from the wallet’s viewing key, the secret a wallet uses to spot payments sent to it, using one-way elliptic-curve math similar to what protects bitcoin and ether wallets.
Ordinary computers can’t run that math in reverse, but a large enough quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm, a method published in 1994 for exactly that job, could theroretically work backward from the address to the key.
That’s the real threat hanging over Satoshi-era bitcoin, whose public keys already sit onchain for anyone to copy. Last week, Google said its Willow quantum chip had produced near-perfect versions of one of the components such an attack would burn through, a step toward a machine powerful enough to try it.
Quantum computers capable of that are still likely years away (and no one has a firm timeline for when one could be built), but it’s a problem developers across the industry are rushing to solve.
One key for every swap
Zcash’s architecture gives it a problem of its own. A Zcash wallet can generate many addresses that look unrelated to each other, but they normally share one viewing key.
An attacker who cracks that key from a single published address could link every payment the account ever received and read the amounts and the private notes, or memos, attached to them.
Spending takes a separate key, so the funds themselves would stay safe. Zakura’s fix gives each swap its own viewing key and leaves the spending key with the user’s main account. An attacker who someday cracks a refund address on NEAR would see only the payments tied to that one swap.
The design also deals with a practical snag.
A wallet that has made hundreds of swaps would end up with hundreds of keys, and restoring it from a backup would mean scanning the entire Zcash chain with every one of them.
Zakura’s answer is a database the wallet can query privately using a technique called private information retrieval. The wallet asks where its refunds landed, and the database answers without learning which addresses the wallet asked about.
As such, no quantum computer capable of recovering these keys has been demonstrated yet. Zakura says wallets built on its open-source libraries, including Vizor, could add the feature in the coming weeks, with hardware wallets following once their firmware supports it.
That would put the fix in users’ hands ahead of the January target Zcash developers set for quantum-resistant payments earlier this month.

- A Bitcoin wallet dormant since 2013 transferred all 411.45 of its coins, now worth about $34 million, to a new address on Sunday.

A bitcoin 
On Sunday, the wallet moved all 411.45 of its BTC to a new address, according to blockchain data from Arkham Intelligence. At today’s price of about $82,600 per coin, that stash is worth roughly $34 million. When the owner first acquired those coins, the entire balance was worth just $54,000.
This awakening is part of a broader trend of historic supply shifting wallets this month. Just a day prior, two other wallets dormant for over a decade moved a combined 417 Bitcoin, and the week before, a large whale wallet static since the pre-Covid crash migrated its funds.
The pattern is highly reminiscent of 2025, when isolated mega-whales repeatedly woke up from a prolonged slumber. Just like last year, these sudden movements of long-dormant supply tend to spark speculation about a potential sale. But, as was the case then, most of the coins have been moved to new private wallets, a sign of custodial maintenance rather than an impending market dump.
The specific wallet behind Sunday's move received the bulk of its funds, some 411 BTC, on Sept. 11, 2013. Back then the cryptocurrency traded around $131. Over the next 13 years, the owner didn't buy, sell, or move a single coin. They simply sat tight as the asset's value skyrocketed more than 600 times, holding through three halvings, the 2017 boom, the 2022 FTX collapse, and the launch of spot bitcoin ETFs in 2024.
While the owner remained completely inactive, the wallet itself did see some activity over the years. Dozens of tiny deposits trickled in, each worth less than a dollar. Several came from addresses that Arkham labels as phishing. It’s a common scam tactic known as “address poisoning.” Fraudsters send trace amounts of crypto ("dust") to high-value wallets, hoping the owner will accidentally copy the scammer's address from their transaction history during a future transfer.
The whale didn't fall for it.
At 18:23 UTC on Sunday, the owner sent the entire fortune to a new address, paying a transaction fee of just 337 satoshis, a fraction of a single cent.
So far, the funds have not been moved to an exchange. The new destination wallet has only received this single transfer and has not initiated any outgoing transactions. That lack of movement points to routine custodial housekeeping rather than a market sell-off.
The original 2013 wallet relied on an outdated address format, whereas the new destination utilizes SegWit (P2WPKH type), which is the modern standard that offers better security and lower transaction fees. Long-dormant holders frequently migrate to these upgraded formats to secure their assets before making any major financial moves.

- Crypto vault deposits have grown from $4 billion at the start of last year to more than $10 billion, according to the Financial Times.

Crypto lending vaults have attracted more than $10 billion in deposits, as investors seek returns on their digital assets, according to the Financial Times.
Deposits have risen from $4 billion at the start of last year, highlighting growing demand for strategies that put stablecoins and other tokens to work.
Vaults operate through smart contracts on decentralized finance platforms. Each has a “curator”, effectively an investment manager, who selects lending strategies, sets risk limits and collects fees. Returns typically range from 3% to 10%, although riskier strategies can generate as much as 20% or more.
The appeal comes with considerable risks. Loans can be backed by illiquid tokens, crypto-backed stablecoins or tokenized private credit, leaving depositors exposed if collateral loses value or becomes difficult to sell.
Automatic liquidations can intensify market declines, while hacks, coding errors and flawed pricing mechanisms create additional vulnerabilities. Publicly accessible smart contracts offer transparency, but investors may focus on headline yields without understanding the underlying exposure.
Fintech companies, digital asset treasury businesses and hedge funds are among the main depositors, according to the article.
Bitcoin backed lender Two Prime are among the firms entering the market. In September, it rolled out a bitcoin lending vault on Pareto targeting annual yields of 1.5% to 2% through institutional lending. The future of perps in the U.S. may be at stake as the CFTC argues that CME hasn't shown the new policy is hurting it after the agency OK'd its first bitcoin perp.
- The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission is seeking to cast doubt on CME Group's legal challenge to its new perps policy.
- The CFTC filed a brief in court arguing that the derivatives giant hasn't shown it's being harmed by the government's new push into perpetual futures, and without harm, it doesn't have legal standing.
The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission threw open the doors for perpetual futures in the U.S. in May, approving the first bitcoin perp from Kalshi and suggesting that it was open for business on ensuring a domestic surge in such contracts. But the CME Group objected in court, and the CFTC has responded in court that the derivatives giant has no right to get in the way.
"Allegations of increased competition, without any plausible inference of an imminent financial injury," don't give CME the legal standing to challenge the CFTC's actions, the agency said in a brief filed on Friday, noting that volume in crypto futures at the CME has actually risen since its policy shift.
Perp contracts had soared overseas, becoming a major form of transaction in crypto derivatives, and the CFTC's move sought to clarify how the market could get rolling in the U.S. The agency — in response to President Donald Trump's aggressive crypto agenda that included bringing perps into domestic trading — said it'll regulate the products on a case-by-case basis as futures.
Perps allow traders to speculate on the future price of an asset with a typically leveraged position, and the contracts don't come with a built-in expiration.
But CME, which operates the leading global venues for derivatives trading, has insisted the contracts are not futures, because they have no end date. They're really swaps, the company's argument would have it, which would come with an entirely different regulatory approach. Spokespeople for CME didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the CFTC's latest filing.
The CFTC first asked a federal judge to dismiss CME's case last month, and this latest filing details its argument against the company's legal standing.
"CME must plausibly allege an actual or imminent increase in competition," the CFTC argued. "CME has not even done that."
The agency argued that CME has been telling investors that it hasn't heard of a demand for perps and that they aren't substitutes for the futures it's offering.
"CME cannot have it one way with the court and another way with the investing public on earnings calls," the CFTC contended in its brief.
Jaret Seiberg, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, argued in a Monday client note that CME may still have the edge, in both its standing as a competitor and its argument that perps may be appropriately treated as swaps. However, the clock is ticking on the new market.
"What increasingly concerns us is the growth in perps while the litigation is playing out," Seiberg wrote. "If this growth continues, it could create complications in trying to unwind this market if the CME prevails in the lawsuit."

The Coinbase allegations expose Bitcoin's corporate governance gap. The Coinbase allegations expose Bitcoin's corporate governance gap
Corporate adoption of bitcoin will stall as long as companies can't show who controls the money, who approves its movement, or whether it's still there, argues Onramp CEO Michael Tanguma.
BlockTower Capital founder Ari Paul publicly accused Coinbase of losing roughly $25 million of his firm's assets and concealing hacks totaling more than $1 billion across a dozen institutions. Coinbase flatly denies it, Paul says active litigation prevents him from publishing his evidence, and the industry has spent the weeks since arguing about who is telling the truth.
The argument misses the most uncomfortable fact in the story: nobody outside the two parties involved can check. That is a strange place to land for an industry built on an asset designed so that no one would have to take anyone's word for anything. A custodian holding assets for much of the market stands accused of billion-dollar concealment, and the only tools available for evaluating the claim are the accuser's credibility and the custodian's word. The lesson for every company holding bitcoin, or deciding whether to, is that bitcoin on a balance sheet presents a controls problem, and until a custody arrangement can answer the same questions a board asks about the company’s bank and brokerage accounts, who can move the money and who signs off, stories like this one will stay unanswerable.
The questions no board can answer
Every other account a company touches comes with governance as a default. A corporate bank account has named users, defined roles, approval rules on withdrawals and an audit trail that a controller can hand to an auditor. A brokerage account has the same. The moment a business buys bitcoin, all of that disappears into one of two places: a single exchange login or a hardware wallet in somebody's drawer.
Boards have noticed, and they’re asking questions. Who can move the asset? Who approves the movement? What happens when the person holding the credentials quits, gets phished, or dies? These are not hypotheticals. QuadrigaCX’s chief executive died in 2018, holding the only keys, and roughly $190 million in customer assets went with him, as the Ontario Securities Commission later documented. Prime Trust discovered in December 2021 that it could not open its own legacy wallets, and still could not 18 months later when Nevada moved to put it into receivership. Across most of the industry, the honest answer to all these questions is a shrug. Companies that wanted bitcoin on the balance sheet have walked away at exactly this point. When Deloitte asked 200 CFOs at billion-dollar companies what was holding them back, the complexity of accounting and controls came in at 42%, within a point of price volatility. The asset was rarely the hard part.
The problem is more acute now than at any point in Bitcoin's history, because the threat landscape is compounding from two directions. Bitcoin turns holders into physical targets, and that hasn't waited for a new price high. Jameson Lopp's public tracker now logs more than 360 known physical attacks since 2014, including 86 in 2025 and more than 60 so far this year. Coinbase made the risk concrete last year when criminals bribed its support staff and stole customer data, including names, addresses and balance information. The company estimated the breach could cost $400 million; security researchers called it a wake-up call because stolen account data exposes holders to real-world coercion.
On the digital side, artificial intelligence has industrialized the attack: cloned voices on the phone with the finance team, phishing emails indistinguishable from the chief executive's, social engineering that improves monthly. A business holding a bearer asset on a single credential carries that entire surface area on behalf of its employees and owners, for an asset where losses are often permanent.
Why the current fixes fail
The industry's existing answers all concentrate risk instead of distributing it. Self-custody concentrates it on one person, which is why corporate self-custody collapses into key ceremonies at every hire and departure and a controller praying the keyholder never leaves angry. Exchange custody concentrates it on one company, with the client holding neither the keys nor any way to see behind the login. Audits, trust charters and SOC reports test the custodian's own books and processes. None of them gives the client named users, approval rules on withdrawals, or a way to confirm the asset is there without asking. The shutdown of BitMEX after 11 years was a reminder of how routinely single institutions simply end. Proof-of-reserves attestations, the industry's favorite half measure, show a snapshot of assets without showing controls, and say nothing about who can move what tomorrow.
The durable fix uses properties bitcoin already has. Multiple signatures are native to the protocol, which means keys can be generated and held by independent regulated institutions, with no single institution able to move or lose the asset, the company holding legal title, named users with defined roles, approval policies on every withdrawal, and an audit trail a board can actually read.
Institutions are already moving in this direction. When Morgan Stanley designed custody for its proposed bitcoin ETF, it named two custodians rather than one, a sign that relying on a single custodian is now a live concern at the top of the market. But splitting custody only goes halfway. The real test is whether the owner can see for itself what it holds, without taking any custodian's word for it. Bitcoin makes that possible, and a custody setup that doesn't take advantage of it leaves the owner exactly where Coinbase's clients are today, waiting for someone to tell them the truth.
Single-custodians are, admittedly, convenient
The fair objection is that single-custodian arrangements exist for good reasons. They're simple: one counterparty to vet, one contract, one integration, and for many companies that simplicity is worth a lot. Spreading custody across independent institutions is harder than it sounds, requiring coordination, shared standards and operational discipline the industry spent its first 15 years avoiding.
Both points are true, and neither weakens the case. Simplicity is only an advantage if what's being simplified can be checked. A single custodian that can't show its clients what it holds hasn't removed complexity; it has hidden it. The cost of that only shows up when a question like the one facing Coinbase lands, and nobody outside can answer it. A financial system in which a billion-dollar question about client assets can't be settled from the outside has failed at the exact thing bitcoin was invented to fix. Building something better than a single point of trust is hard, and it's also the industry's actual job.
Verification was the whole point
Corporate adoption of bitcoin will stall as long as companies hold it in custody that can't show who controls the money, who approves its movement, or whether it's still there, which is exactly the gap the Coinbase allegations exposed. Boards do not need to become bitcoin experts to force the change; they only need to ask what they already ask of every other account, and add one more question: what survives the departure of any single person or institution. Any custody arrangement that cannot answer those questions clearly is a risk disclosure waiting to be written. A decade from now, the industry will look back with astonishment that it invented a radically new form of money and spent years custodying it behind a single login. The sooner custody is built so that no single party can lose, move, or lie about what it holds, the sooner the question hanging over the industry becomes impossible to ask.

Solana transactions could soon become irreversible in just 150 milliseconds, or roughly 40 times faster than today, as the network switches on its Alpenglow upgrade on Wednesday.
The upgrade changes how validators, the computers that process transactions and vote on which ones are valid, agree with each other.
Today, every validator writes its votes straight onto the blockchain like any other transaction, and a payment isn’t locked in until enough of them stack up — which takes about six seconds.
Alpenglow pulls that voting off the chain and bundles votes into certificates that can lock in a transaction in one or two rounds. If the 150-millisecond target holds up on mainnet, a Solana transaction would be settled in less time than it takes to blink.
Six seconds is a long time in a fast market, where a price can move before a trade is locked in, and exchanges and payment apps make users wait before treating a deposit as done.
But cutting that to a fraction of a second gets Solana much closer to the feel of a card payment or a trade on a centralized exchange (Ethereum, by comparison, takes roughly 13 minutes to reach full finality).
"Solana's transaction count is going to look a lot lower this week, and people will ask if something's wrong. It isn't,” shared Robin Nordnes, CEO and founder of Raiku, which builds trading infrastructure on Solana, in an email.. “Most of what got counted before was validators voting, and that's off-chain now. The trading's all still there.”
“For desks, faster finality is nice, but it was never the bottleneck. Being close to where the block is built still is,” he added.
Read More: Solana is about to halve its block times as final 200-millisecond upgrade nears
Validators also get a cheaper bill. They currently burn through about 2 SOL a day on vote fees, a cost that doubled after Solana recently cut its slot times, the window each block gets, to about 200 milliseconds.
Alpenglow scraps those fees in favor of a flat entry charge called a validator admission ticket, set at 0.8 SOL per epoch, a period of about 24 hours. That’s roughly 60% cheaper.
Getting here wasn’t smooth.
The test network was wiped and restarted from scratch six times since launching in early May, and one attempt to migrate to the new system failed network-wide and had to be rolled back, according to a post from Galaxy Digital, one of roughly 100 validator operators on the test network. A later migration went through, clearing the way for Wednesday’s launch.
None of that put real money at risk, since it all happened on a network built for exactly that kind of breakage.
The switch is set for the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, with the actual change at slot 459,653,000 after a 5,000-slot transition.

- Monero futures open interest has surpassed $300 million, nearing January’s record of about $320 million and increasing the risk of a sharp, liquidation-driven price move.
- Open interest has also climbed to a five-week high of 515,730 XMR as monero’s spot price recently topped $600, suggesting leveraged bets are growing alongside the rally.
- A similar buildup in January preceded a 66 percent plunge, when monero fell from about $790 to below $300 as long positions were forcibly closed.
Leveraged bets are building up in monero (XMR) futures, raising the odds of a sharp, sudden move in the price.
Monero (XMR) is a cryptocurrency built for privacy. Its transactions are hard to trace and at the market cap of $10.9 billion, it is the second-largest privacy coin in the world.
Notional open interest, or the dollar value of the number of active monero futures bets, has risen past $300 million, approaching the January peak of around $320 million, according to data source SoSoValue. Futures are contracts that let traders bet on a coin’s price without owning it. To date, the tally has topped $300 million only a few times, all this year.
“The last Time we reached that amount of Open Interest was in Jan 2026. Monero Crashed 66% in the next 20 days. I Smell a very big Liquidation Event on XMR,” said pseudonymous crypto analyst Doctor Profit, who correctly called BTC’s 2025 top and pivoted to accumulation in July this year.
Open interest is tracked in dollars and in coins. Traders use the two differently. The dollar figure shows the current size of the market’s positions and lets traders compare monero with other cryptocurrencies. Liquidations are also typically reported in dollars, so a larger dollar figure points to a larger potential wave of forced selling. Open interest is also rising in coin terms. At 515.73K XMR, it is at a five-week high and up sharply from 400K XMR a week ago.
Liquidations, or forced closure of positions by exchanges, happen because futures involve leverage, in which a trader puts up a small deposit, called margin, to control a much larger position.
This leverage boosts gains when the market moves as expected, but when it doesn’t, the margin is eaten away. At some point, the exchange steps in and closes the position to prevent the trader’s losses from exceeding the collateral they posted and to protect the exchange from unpaid losses.
Traders betting on a rise, called longs, get liquidated when the price falls. The liquidation, in turn, adds to selling pressure in the market. This is especially true when most traders are long. In such cases, a slight price decline can trigger mass liquidation of longs and a price crash.
That’s what happened in January when open interest hit a record high alongside a price rise, reflecting an overcrowding of longs. The spot price hit a high of around $790 on Jan. 14. By the first week of February, it had crashed to under $300. This was characterized by liquidation of longs worth several million dollars, according to Coinglass.
This time too, the spot price has risen with the open interest. Monero recently topped $600, the highest since January.
Whether history repeats remains to be seen.

The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is the first of several federal agencies to finish writing regulations under the act.
- The U.S. agency that regulates national banks and trusts has issued the first final rule putting the GENIUS Act into place in January, though a number of other regulators are still working on other parts of the implementation.
- The section on stablecoin yield doesn't offer a lot of detail on what activity may fall under the law's wide prohibition of such yield from issuers, but the crypto industry has already interpreted GENIUS to permit the rewards programs that have become commonplace with stablecoin activity on exchanges.
- The final rule states that pre-existing rewards programs won't get special treatment as the OCC assesses which ones pass regulatory muster.
U.S. crypto exchanges that have long been giving people rewards for usings stablecoins will have to get the agency to sign off on those existing programs, according to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the first federal banking regulator to issue a final rule under the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act.
The OCC, which oversees U.S. national banks and trusts that will play a central role in the issuance of stablecoins under the law, issued a final rule on Wednesday to establish the regulations under which the firms that issue the dollar-based tokens will operate — including in their third-party relationships with the exchanges on which their stablecoins change hands.
The agency — an independent bureau of the Treasury Department — has declined to offer examples or illustrations of what type of rewards operations may run afoul of the GENIUS Act, which declared that payments to customers made "solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin" won't be allowed. The industry, which won't get any safe harbors for existing programs, will just have to test the agency's case-by-case oversight to get a better sense of the rule, which is set to go live on January 18.
The regulator said it "will apply the language of the statute to the facts and circumstances of any particular arrangement." However, the agency did suggest that the word "solely" in the prohibition is carrying a lot of weight, and that a reward that "might be made, at least in part, for other reasons" would fall outside the ban in the GENIUS Act.
Payment stablecoins hew to the value of the U.S. dollar and are designed — as suggested by the name — to maintain a steady value in a crypto industry in which other assets are known to be famously volatile. The sector is currently led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, but a number of entrants have begun crowding into the space.
Wednesday's extensive rule establishes the start-to-finish process for regulated firms and foreign companies to issue stablecoins in the U.S. and for how firms will keep custody of them. But the rule is also meant to operate alongside a number of similar rules still being worked on by other agencies, and this effort leaves aside the Bank Secrecy Act components that will be handled by other arms of the Treasury.
"The OCC’s final rule carries that landmark legislation forward, providing a clear, practical foundation for private-sector innovation, competition, and American leadership in digital assets,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent in a statement.
But the questions of yield have long swirled at the center of stablecoin regulation.
Yield saga
A number of financial firms, such as U.S. exchange Coinbase, have well-established rewards programs — akin to the customer incentives associated with credit card providers. Some of the highest rates are currently offered by PayPal and Kraken.
The GENIUS Act's ban on the issuers giving anything that looks like interest directly to the holders of their tokens has been a controversial topic and drew a lot of comments to the agency after its earlier proposal.
The programs have been declared by bankers to be a dangerous competitive threat to the customer deposits at the core of their business model. The banks felt so strongly about this that they lobbied to force further changes of the GENIUS Act into the later Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, and they continued fighting the point so vigorously that the Clarity Act couldn't muster unanimous Republican support when it failed to advance in a key Senate vote last month.
Without the amendments that had long been negotiated by bankers, the crypto industry, lawmakers and the White House, the unchanged GENIUS Act remains the only standard for how exchanges such as Coinbase should govern their rewards programs. Bankers who were concerned that the law's language would undermine their deposits are still stuck with that language, though bank deposits have continued to grow after the explosion of interest in stablecoins.
The new OCC rule noted that many commenters suggested the agency needed to consider that the Clarity Act may still overhaul GENIUS on this point (though odds of further action on the markets structure bill are long). But the regulator responded, "Unless and until such legislation passes, the OCC must implement the GENIUS Act’s yield prohibition, as enacted."
When the OCC first proposed its rule earlier this year, there was some uncertainty in the industry about how the agency would police the GENIUS Act's anti-evasion language meant to keep firms from gaming the restrictions on issuers from offering yield or rewards. But the industry has since embraced what it's interpreted as an ongoing legal clearance to offer certain rewards through secondary platforms.
For instance, PayPal offers a 4% return for users of its PYUSD, Coinbase One gives 3.75% on USDC positions and Kraken+ subscribers can make as much as 4.5% on USDG accounts.
"The OCC declines to presume that rewards programs that predated the GENIUS Act comply with the GENIUS Act," according to Wednesday's rule document. "The fact that Congress may have had notice of these rewards programs does not necessarily imply that Congress endorsed them as permissible."
In the final rule, it also took out what it had called "rebuttable presumptions" that assumed specified activities that would violate the rule.
Other agencies
GENIUS' implementation by regulators doesn't stop at the OCC, though that agency has influenced how others are writing their own rules. Though the GENIUS Act had called for a mid-year deadline that none of the regulators met, the Treasury Department, Federal Reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. also have rulemakings underway:
- The FDIC was first out of the gate with application standards late last year, and in April, the agency proposed its approach to regulate state-chartered institutions.
- The Treasury Department also proposed its handling of the law in August, and the industry is carefully monitoring how it will treat foreign issuers, such as Tether. That August action followed a joint proposal in April from the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) that suggested the controls that stablecoin businesses would have to put in place, including abilities to stop or freeze transactions and compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act that governs most of the U.S. financial system.
- Just last month, the Fed issued its own proposals for member banks' subsidiaries that intend to issue stablecoins, including procedures for issuing them and standards for capital and reserves.
The overall effective date of the GENIUS Act was supposed to arrive in January, but it's unlikely all of the required rules will be in place before then, based on the scheduled periods in which the other agencies are still taking public comments.
OCC officials told reporters that the new rule will give "opportunities for a range of institutions," including community banks, to get involved with stablecoins.
The agency said it changed its reserve requirements between the proposed rule and this final one, adopting "a principles-based approach with respect to reserve asset diversification and concentration requirements," which it said is backed by requirements to "ensure a minimum amount of daily liquidity and avoid excessive concentration with respect to a single counterparty."

Real-world assets need fixed-rate lending to scale in DeFi
Fixed-rate lending is the clearest growth lever for real-world assets (RWAs) in decentralized finance (DeFi). It unlocks a strategy that credit desks have run for decades but DeFi has never meaningfully implemented: buy a quality income asset, borrow against it at a locked rate below the asset’s yield and buy more of the asset.
